variants.name: Type-class policy through given instances and using clauses (Scala 3)
variants.idiom_name: type-class policy injected with given/using (context parameters)
variants.implementation_notes: Scala's contextual abstractions are the pattern's Scala form: the policy is a value of a policy trait (trait EvictionPolicy[K] { def pick(keys: List[K]): K }), the host declares a context parameter (class Cache[K, V](using policy: EvictionPolicy[K])) and the compiler injects the policy found in scope, so the binding site is the summoning call site rather than a type argument. given instances are the canonical policy implementations, context bounds shorten signatures, and the standard library ships policies this way (Ordering, Numeric, builders). Because a policy is an ordinary value, a run-time choice remains possible, but the injected default keeps call sites free of policy plumbing when it is not needed.
pitfalls: Given resolution is scope- and import-sensitive: a policy imported in one file changes instantiations elsewhere, and two equally specific givens produce an ambiguity error instead of a silent choice.
Parameterized given defs create a fresh instance per reference (no memoization); performance-sensitive policies should be unconditional objects or lazy vals.
Using clauses are resolved when the call site compiles, so a policy cannot be swapped by configuration without passing it explicitly with `using`.

variants.name: Type-class policy through implicit parameters (Scala 2)
variants.idiom_name: trait policy + implicit parameter or context bound
variants.implementation_notes: The Scala 2 realization: the host takes an implicit parameter (class Cache[K: EvictionPolicy, V]) and policy implementations are implicit objects or defs, resolved by the compiler at the call site. This is the form Scala 3's givens replaced, and it still compiles under Scala 3 because Scala 2 implicits are part of the common subset - choose it for libraries that must cross-build 2.13 and 3, and prefer the given/using form for new Scala 3 code.
pitfalls: Implicit resolution differs between Scala 2 and 3 (priority by inheritance depth versus preference for the most general given, plus recursive-given avoidance), so the same code can select a different policy after migration.
Scala 2 cannot express multiple implicit parameter lists, which forces Aux-object workarounds when a policy itself needs a type parameter.
